content.title: The No. 1 'Big' Colorectal Cancer Symptom a Doctor Monitors in Himself
content.text: Colorectal cancer is especially deadly for younger adults in their 20s, 30s and 40s.It’s now the No. 1 cause of cancer deaths in people under 50, “a troubling shift in who is being affected,” the American Cancer Society warns. High-profile early onset patients include actor James Van Der Beek, who died at 48; and actor Chadwick Boseman, who passed away at 43.As Dr. Derek Ebner, a gastroenterologist at the Mayo Clinic, treats patients with the disease, he thinks about colorectal cancer affecting himself as well.“It definitely crosses my mind,” Ebner tells TODAY.com.“As an individual who is (younger) than age 50, and especially realizing the increasing rates of colorectal cancer have really been observed in those less than age 50 … I have two young boys at home, 8 and 4, so it does bring just a heightened awareness.”He manages the lifestyle factors he can control, such as eating a healthy diet and exercising every day to lower his risk. Getting screened is key as well.Colorectal cancer refers to tumors that arise in the large intestine, and includes both colon and rectal cancers.“The colon is the vast majority of the large intestine,” Ebner says.“The rectum is just that very last portion of the large intestine before something passes into the commode.”Rectal cancer in particular has been on the rise, the American Cancer Society reports, now accounting for almost one‑third, or 32%, of all colorectal cancer cases. It was the underlying cause of death of actor Catherine O’Hara.The treatment is slightly different depending on the location of the tumor. After colon cancer is staged, patients then often undergo surgery — unless the disease has spread to other parts of the body, he notes. With rectal cancer, staging is often followed by chemotherapy or radiation before any surgery.It’s important to pay attention to the warning signs to catch the cancer before it spreads, Ebner emphasizes.“If you capture things early, survival is wonderful. If it's early colorectal cancer, survival at five years is over 90%,” he says.“If it's captured later, that’s where the outcome is different.”Here are colorectal cancer symptoms the doctor pays attention to in his own body:Blood With a Bowel MovementThis warning sign is one of the two “big ones” when it comes to symptoms most linked to cases of early onset colorectal cancer, Ebner says.“For me, as an individual who's (younger) than 50, blood from the bottom is something I'm very mindful of,” he notes.“The scary thing is in my practice, where I really see folks that come in intentionally to Mayo for discussion on their diagnosis of colorectal cancer, there's a lot of individuals who had assumed that they were just experiencing bleeding because of a hemorrhoid. And because of that assumption, they did not seek early medical evaluation.”Bright red blood in particular — whether it shows up as droplets in the toilet bowl or on the toilet paper after wiping — is worth bringing up to your doctor, he notes.Ebner urges people to look at their stool before flushing. A streak of blood on the outside might mean the bleeding source is close to the bottom of the digestive tract, which could be a hemorrhoid or a rectal tumor, he notes.Blood that's mixed into the stool may indicate the bleeding source is more towards the start of the colon.“If you observe it, it's best to let your health care team know and not leave something to chance,” he advises.Abdominal PainThis is the second symptom of the two “big ones” Ebner pays particular attention to.Oftentimes, especially with early onset colorectal cancer, the abdominal pain tends to be along the left side of the abdomen, either in the left lower quadrant or the left upper quadrant, he notes.It can feel like constant discomfort or a fullness, and may be caused by a tumor in the digestive tract. When the pain is exacerbated with movement, the cause is usually a blockage.“Stool, for example, normally is going to pass freely along the entire length of the large intestine. But if there is a bulky mass that is limiting the ability for stool to go by, that's going to lead to fullness, pressure and discomfort, and that's what one would perceive as the abdominal pain," Ebner says.Unproductive Urge to Go to the BathroomThis symptom may be caused by rectal cancer that invades the sphincter muscles and induces the urge to have a bowel movement when there’s no stool to pass.Similarly, the mass could be occupying space higher in the rectum and lead to an unproductive urge for defecation. Iron Deficiency AnemiaThe cause can be slow blood loss that you might not see in your stool because the mass that’s bleeding is at the very start of the colon,This eventually causes low red blood cell counts, or anemia.“You might be feeling more fatigued along the way, or those low blood counts are seen from just some routine lab monitoring,” Ebner says.Unexplained Weight LossA rectal cancer patient recently told TODAY.com she unexpectedly lost 26 pounds over about six months before her diagnosis.One study found 38% of colon cancer patients whose disease was found early experienced unintentional weight loss. That number rose to 50% if the cancer had already spread.When to Get HelpIf you have any colorectal cancer symptoms, the easiest next step is to reach out to your primary care provider, Ebner advises.If you don’t have one, he suggests calling your health insurance company to get suggestions for doctors who are in network, asking friends and family members for a referral or going to an urgent care to see if doctors there might check out the warning signs or help navigate the next steps.Screening is a key part of prevention — most people should start soon after turning 45, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It can be done with stool tests, a colonoscopy and other methods.“The best one is the one that gets done,” Ebner says.TODAY.com’s Symptom Check series features doctors, specialists and health experts who reveal the warning signs they’d look for in their own body when it comes to cancer and other diseases.
